# Welcome to the era of embodied AI: Introducing AA-Robotics v0.1

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

## Introducing AA-Robotics v0.1

Since the beginning of 2026, frontier language models have made enormous progress in their ability to control robot arms. We now believe that the future of robotics is likely to involve strong generalist agents, and conclude that tracking progress of language models for robotics tasks is going to be important - even if frontier language models are unsuitable for production robotics use on their own.

AA-Robotics v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this - language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a robot arm. Each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective for each task.

We find that frontier language models in coding agent harnesses have indeed recently become capable of directly manipulating robot arms for simple tasks. Today, they are far too slow and expensive for any kind of production usage - nearly two orders of magnitude worse than human baselines. We expect this to change quickly.

GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1 with a score of 69, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. GPT-6 Astra took 30 minutes and cost $16.36 on average per task.

### AA-Robotics Score

Each attempt is scored out of 100: completing the task scores 100, and a partial result earns points for the progress made.

## The eight tasks

AA-Robotics v0.1 initially includes eight tabletop tasks, modeled on everyday activities, to evaluate a range of robotics capabilities: control and dexterity, such as precise grasping and handling objects, spatial reasoning, such as understanding how objects interact with one another, and adaptability, measuring how models respond to the unexpected.

## How AA-Robotics works

Models run in an isolated container with brief instructions: how to reach the robot arm (via a simple HTTP API), which arm it is (a Hiwonder NexArm, with no further specifications), and how to submit an attempt as complete. They can view the scene through four cameras, three mounted around the table and one on the arm’s wrist, and can write and run code in the container to plan and send movements.

Once a model has submitted a task for review, the end state is graded against the task’s pass criteria. A pass scores 100, with points awarded for partial success in the case of an incomplete task. All task attempts are zero-shot.

## Time & cost

Today’s language models are roughly 100 times slower than a human on AA-Robotics v0.1, taking about half an hour per task compared with a human average of 20 seconds. In aggregate, four of the five models tested look similar, at about 30 minutes per task, while Gemini 4 Argon is the slowest at 52 minutes. However, these averages hide large differences between tasks.

GPT-6 Astra pressed the red button in 2.2 minutes, whereas Claude Fable 5.1 spent about ten minutes understanding and planning before its first action. The largest difference came on the crocodile placement task, where GPT-6.1 Sol declared itself complete after five minutes, compared with 45 for Claude Opus 5.5, a ninefold difference. Across all tasks, Gemini 4 Argon was the slowest to act, spending an average of 21 minutes observing and reasoning before its first action, nearly twice as long as any other model.

### Time per Task

### AA-Robotics Score vs. Time per Task

The gap between humans and models is narrower on cost: the most cost-effective model costs about ten times as much as a person paid the average US hourly wage, against nearly 100 times as long on time. Between models, GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest, at $1.93 per task on average, while GPT-6 Astra, the most expensive, costs $16.36, more than eight times as much as Sol, for a score only four points higher (69 against 65). Given the novelty of the arm and scene, and the large volume of visual information the models must process, most of the cost lands on input: 70% of the spend goes on context.

## How each model spent its time

As expected, models spend a large portion of the initial task time calibrating the arm and understanding the scene, continuing this up until taking the first action. After this point, the majority of time is spent planning movement, with relatively short, precise arm movements between each longer planning step. Camera views and note writing are relatively small fractions of the overall time.

Interestingly, models often continue to refine their attempts long after reaching a passing state. GPT-6.1 Sol, for example, builds a passing tower after ~17 minutes, only to subsequently fail the task. It remains to be seen how models will improve their ability to reason about task completion in physical space.

## Physical accuracy

Grasping and fine manipulation were key skills to test in AA-Robotics v0.1, as they point the way not only to more precise control tasks, but more importantly to tool use and the far wider range of capabilities it unlocks.

GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 performed best with the highest proportion of successful attempts (~45%), indicating a degree of close control, whilst GPT-6.1 Sol, scored worst, at 28%. Gemini 4 Argon fell in between at 36%, with many of its misses closing just above or beside the block it was reaching for.

### Outcome of Every Grasp Attempt

- Successful Grasp

- Missed, Partial, or Wrong-Object Grasp

Grasps were attempted in the Place Crocodile, Pour Drink, Tidy Box, Match Shapes, Build Tower, and Measure Box tasks. Successful is defined as holding the intended object through its lift or carry, and missed, partial, or wrong-object where the gripper did not close on the object, closed on it before it slipped, dropped, or could not be lifted, or took a different object by mistake.

# Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5

Index v5 features 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New to the Intelligence Index:

➤ FrontierCode 2.0: Cognition's newly-launched private benchmark of real-world coding tasks, graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change

➤ Terminal-Bench-Science: 70 agentic scientific research tasks, run in a terminal environment

Upgraded:

➤ HLE-Diamond (replacing Humanity's Last Exam): a refined 1,000-question version of Humanity's Last Exam, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge questions

➤ AA-Omniscience v1.1: an updated dataset with saturated and public set questions removed, new questions added, and ambiguous or erroneous questions revised

➤ CritPt v2: a private, 40-question hard subset of CritPt v2, revised by the CritPt authors and run with a code-execution tool

Staying in the Index: AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf and Terminal-Bench 4.0

Removed from the Index: GDPval-AA v2.1, SciCode, and AA-LCR v1.1

Intelligence Index v5 weights:

➤ Knowledge Work (25%): AA-Briefcase (15%), AutomationBench-AA (5%), and GDP.pdf (5%)

➤ Coding (25%): FrontierCode 2.0 (15%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (10%)

➤ Science (25%): Terminal-Bench-Science (15%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (10%)

➤ General (25%): AA-Omniscience v1.1 15% (10% accuracy, 5% non-hallucination) and HLE-Diamond (10%)

Key results:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55): Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five models. Gemini 4 Argon (high) is next at 50

➤ The open weights gap widens from 3 points to 12: Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the top open weights model at 46. Among released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 - 26 points behind the leader and below Claude Haiku 5.5 (max, 36)

➤ Cost per task varies by more than 13x among the leading models: of the 10 highest-scoring models shown, GPT-6.1 Terra (max) is the cheapest at $0.96 per Intelligence Index task and Claude Fable 5.1 (max) the most expensive at $13.04

FrontierCode 2.0 is the latest update of Cognition's private coding benchmark. Launched earlier today, it comprises 132 tasks in real open-source repositories, graded on whether a maintainer would merge the agent's change. An attempt that fails any blocking check scores 0, and the tasks stay private to avoid contamination. We run every task three times in Stirrup, our agentic harness.

Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 46%, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max), GPT-6.1 Terra (max) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max), all at 42%. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) is the highest-scoring open weights model at 28%, 18 points behind the leader.

Terminal-Bench-Science tests whether agents can carry out scientific research workflows in a terminal. Experts curate and review each task, and a task passes only if every one of its tests passes.

GPT-6 Astra (max) leads at 63%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 59% and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 58%. Scores drop off sharply below the leaders: the best open weights model, Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released), scores 34%, and Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) scores 20%. The best open weights model with released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max), scores 13%, and most open weights models we benchmarked score under 10%.

HLE-Diamond replaces Humanity's Last Exam in the Index. It is the refined 1,000-question version of Humanity's Last Exam from the Center for AI Safety (CAIS) and Scale AI, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 68%, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) at 64% and Claude Fable 5.1 (max) at 60%.

Knowledge questions are harder than reasoning questions for the leading models: Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) both score 78% on reasoning, compared with 58% and 50% on knowledge.

AA-Omniscience v1.1 is a cleaned version of our knowledge and hallucination benchmark, with saturated and public set questions removed, new questions added, and ambiguous or erroneous questions revised. Scores are mostly aligned with v1, with models scoring on average 2 points lower on the AA-Omniscience v1.1 Index (median 0.6). We’ve also released a new public subset on Hugging Face, AA-Omniscience-Public-v1.1, recalibrated to ensure accuracy, hallucination rate, and overall performance are consistent between the public and private sets.

The Index scores CritPt v2 on a private 40-question hard subset: the 70 research-level physics questions, minus the 30 that seven frontier models solved in all five attempts at launch. Models work in an offline Python sandbox in Stirrup, our agentic harness.

GPT-6 Astra leads at 72% on high effort, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol at 69% on max effort. Claude Opus 5.5 (max), the top model in the Index overall, scores 61%. Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the highest-scoring open weights model at 45%.

v5 leaves significant room for progress across all nine evaluations, and no single model leads them all. Of the models we measured, Claude Opus 5.5 leads three, and five other models lead the remaining six:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5: FrontierCode 2.0 (46%), HLE-Diamond (68%) and AA-Omniscience v1.1 (48)

➤ GPT-6 Astra: Terminal-Bench-Science (63%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (72%)

➤ Claude Sonnet 5.5: AA-Briefcase (1812 Elo)

➤ Kimi K3.1 Pro: Terminal-Bench 4.0 (67%)

➤ Gemini 4 Argon: AutomationBench-AA (78%)

➤ Muse Wonder Full: GDP.pdf (33% all-pass)

Open weights models fall further behind in v5. The best, Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released), scores 46, 12 points behind the leader, compared with a 3-point gap in v4.3. Of models with released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) score highest at 32, and Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) outscores all of them.

The gap is widest on HLE-Diamond and Terminal-Bench-Science, where Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 37% and 34%, compared with 68% for Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and 63% for GPT-6 Astra (max).

Cost varies widely among the leading models. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) costs $10.04 per Intelligence Index task, GPT-6 Astra (max) $6.24 and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) $1.27. GPT-6.1 Sol (max) scores within 4 points of Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at about an eighth of the cost per task.

Effort settings matter more in v5 than in v4.3. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 35 at low effort and 58 at max, at 10x the cost per Intelligence Index task ($0.98 vs $10.04). Claude Sonnet 5.5 spans 29 points from low to max, up from 20 in v4.3, and GPT-6.1 Sol's spread doubles from 10 to 20 points.

v5 tasks demand substantially more work from models. Every model we measured generates more output tokens per Intelligence Index task than in v4.3, with the median rising by two thirds, from 35k to 59k.

➤ Agentic evaluations account for most token use: Terminal-Bench-Science, Terminal-Bench 4.0, AA-Briefcase and FrontierCode 2.0 make up 55% of the Index weight but a median ~90% of output tokens

➤ Terminal-Bench-Science is the most token-intensive: it accounts for about a third of output Tokens per Task on its own

# Artificial Analysis Intelligence Benchmarking Methodology

### Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index combines a comprehensive suite of evaluation datasets to assess language model capabilities across reasoning, knowledge, math, and programming.

It is a helpful synthesis of overall language model intelligence and can be used to compare language models. Like all evaluation metrics, it has limitations and may not apply directly to every use case. However, we are confident that it is a more useful synthesis comparison between language models than any other metric in existence today.

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 incorporates 9 evaluations: AA-Briefcase v1.1, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf, FrontierCode 2.0, Terminal-Bench 4.0, AA-Omniscience v1.1, HLE-Diamond, CritPt v2 (Hard Subset), and Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1.0. Our methodology emphasizes fairness and real-world applicability.

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a primarily text-based, English-language evaluation suite. We benchmark models for image inputs, speech inputs and multilingual performance separately to the Intelligence Index evaluation suite.

Intelligence Index evaluation suite

The Intelligence Index is calculated as a weighted average across four categories: Knowledge Work (25%), Coding (25%), Science (25%), and General (25%). Category membership and per-evaluation weights are shown below.

Beyond the Intelligence Index suite, we run a range of additional evaluations covering multilingual, visual, mathematical, and other capabilities. These are reported separately and are not included in the Intelligence Index score.

Artificial Analysis Multilingual Index: Represents the multilingual ability of models. This is based on the Global-MMLU-Lite evaluation across supported languages. We support the following languages:

- 🇬🇧 English

- 🇨🇳 Chinese

- 🇮🇳 Hindi

- 🇪🇸 Spanish

- 🇫🇷 French

- 🇸🇦 Arabic

- 🇧🇩 Bangla

- 🇵🇹 Portuguese

- 🇮🇩 Indonesian

- 🇯🇵 Japanese

- 🇰🇪 Swahili

- 🇩🇪 German

- 🇰🇷 Korean

- 🇮🇹 Italian

- 🇳🇬 Yoruba

- 🇲🇲 Burmese

Our evaluation approach is guided by four core principles:

- Standardized: All models are evaluated under identical conditions with consistent prompting strategies, temperature settings, and evaluation criteria.

- Unbiased: We employ evaluation techniques that avoid unfairly penalizing models for answers that correctly follow the instructions in our prompts. This includes using clear prompts, robust answer extraction methods, and flexible answer validation to accommodate valid variations in model outputs.

- Zero-Shot Instruction Prompted: We evaluate using clear instructions without examples or demonstrations, testing models' ability to follow directions without few-shot learning. This approach aligns with modern instruction-tuned and chat style models.

- Transparent: We disclose our methodology, including prompt templates, evaluation criteria, and limitations.

We test all evals with the following settings:

- Temperature: 0 for non-reasoning models, 0.6 for reasoning models (unless another temperature is recommended by the model lab)

- Maximum output tokens:

- Non-reasoning models: 16,384 tokens (adjusted downward where models have a smaller context window, or lower maximum output tokens cap)

- Reasoning models: Maximum output tokens allowed, as disclosed by model creators (custom setting for each reasoning model)

- Error handling:

- Automatic retry on API failures (up to 30 attempts)

- All questions that failed all 30 retries are manually reviewed. Results where persistent API failures have caused issues are not published. Errors where all available APIs for proprietary models block a certain question may lower scores (this effect is not material)

- Scoring methodology: We generally use pass@1 scoring across our evaluations, where a model must produce the correct answer on its first attempt. For evaluations with multiple repeats, pass@1 is calculated by aggregating results across all repeats. This is calculated as: where p i = 1 if attempt i is correct, 0 otherwise, and k is the total number of test instances across all repeats.

We maintain internal copies of all evaluation datasets. The sources of our selected datasets are listed below.

For the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index evaluations, we use the token counts reported by each model's API provider where available, to accurately report the cost of running the Intelligence Index. In the rare cases where provider token counts are unavailable, we use a canonical-tokenizer fallback. This contrasts with the approach in performance benchmarking, where we use client-side token counts from the o200k_base tokenizer to standardize token counts for the same text across models. When reporting cache hit rates and cost, we combine these token counts with live measurements of the model's typical cache hit rate, rather than relying on the one-off measurement when the evaluation was run.

We use e2b as our primary sandbox provider for agentic benchmarks.

- Implementation: Each AA-Briefcase scenario is a realistic multi-week business problem, organized as a multi-week workflow that the agent works through in sequence, with 2-5 tasks per week. Although tasks within a scenario share files and context across weeks, models currently complete each task in an independent run, without carrying over their own prior submissions. The agent receives the task description and accessible source files, then produces final deliverable files without live interaction or iterative feedback during execution. Scenario source pools include shared files and week-specific files, mixing real, augmented, and synthetic materials. Source files are designed to include realistic professional artifacts such as Slack exports, spreadsheets, PDFs, interview transcripts, market research, standards documents, app-store pages, board materials, emails, and other business records. Later-week tasks may receive standardized base-case files (the same reference work products given to every model), so each task stays independently runnable while preserving continuity across the week. Model submissions are run with Stirrup in a week-scoped E2B sandbox. Turns: Agents run for up to 500 turns per task. Tools: The agent is given a single code-execution tool that runs shell commands and code inside the sandbox, plus the finish tools below (and a view-image tool when the model supports vision). The sandbox has no internet access, so the agent can only use the provided source files. Sandbox: Each scenario/week sandbox is built from that week's source files, with standard Python packages and system tools for document processing and scientific computing pre-installed. Finish tools: A finish tool, which the agent calls to submit a summary and the absolute paths of its deliverables (validated to be actual files, not directories or missing paths), and an abandon_task_finish (give-up) tool, which it calls with a reason only when it concludes the task is genuinely impossible. Prompts: The prompts used across generation and grading: Agent system prompt: You are an AI agent working on a specific task within a multi-week simulated workplace scenario. Each task is part of a longer workflow; your job is to complete the current task using the tools provided in up to 500 steps, then submit your deliverables. When you are done you must call the `finish` tool as your final step, passing a brief summary of what you accomplished and a list of absolute paths for every deliverable file. If you have genuinely concluded that the task cannot be completed — for example because required inputs are missing, a hard dependency is unavailable, or the request itself is incoherent — call the `abandon_task_finish` tool with a brief reason instead. Do not use it to escape difficulty. You cannot interact with the user during the task. Record any clarifying assumptions you made in your finish summary. Agent task prompt: <execution_context> ## Sandbox You operate inside an isolated Linux container through the `code_exec` tool, which runs shell commands and lets you read, create, and edit files. Commands run as the unprivileged user `user` (UID 1000), starting from `/home/user`. Passwordless `sudo` exists but is rarely needed, since your home directory is fully writable. Every command runs independently: no working directory, environment variable, or other shell state carries over from one call to the next. Prefer absolute paths for both files and commands, and do not navigate with `cd` across calls — a `cd` in one command is gone by the next, so relying on it leaves you silently operating in the wrong place. When a step genuinely needs a different directory, chain it into the same command (e.g. `cd /home/user/work && python build.py`). ## No network The container has no outbound connectivity, and there is no proxy, allowlist, or flag that can turn it on — treat the environment as permanently offline. ### Total Parameters

The total number of trainable weights and biases in the model, expressed in billions. These parameters are learned during training and determine the model's ability to process and generate responses.

### Active Parameters at Inference Time

The number of parameters actually executed during each inference forward pass, expressed in billions. Dense models use all parameters, so active equals total.
